items.value: Only assumption 3 is valid: government programmes are needed for those left behind in economic growth
items.reasoning: The passage opens by asking why mass welfare cannot be left entirely to the markets, and answers that some people never get the opportunity to develop the skills markets demand because they are too poor or too handicapped. That argument only works if something outside the market must provide for them, which is exactly assumption 3. Assumption 1 is the opposite of what the passage argues: it says there is a built-in tension between markets and democracy and that welfare cannot be left to markets, not that democracies rely on markets to become welfare states. Assumption 2 is never made: the passage says markets may lift many from the bottom rungs and may create jobs, but immediately notes that capitalism has always witnessed bursts of unemployment, and it nowhere links growth to democratic effectiveness.

items.value: Being a better citizen today requires societal awareness and life-coping skills alongside academic content, not academic content alone
items.reasoning: The passage is built on a single contrast: schools teach physics, maths and history, but not the caste divide, famine, gender sensitivity or atheism as a choice (societal content), and they do not teach children to ask questions or form opinions, which is why the move to university is painful (life-coping content). Option D names both halves of that contrast and preserves the 'in addition to academic content' structure the passage turns on. Option C is the runner-up and is defensible, but it captures only the citizenship half and states it as a claim about whose responsibility this is, which the passage never argues; it says nothing about the questioning and transition material that occupies the second half. Option A introduces expectations of children and parents, which the passage never mentions. Option B as printed asserts that emphasis on academic achievement DOES give time for development of personality and skills, which contradicts the passage; note that the passage itself carries a printing defect (a semicolon in 'In our schools; we teach') and this option reads as though a negation has been dropped, but it is answered as printed and is wrong either way.

items.value: n = 2; PQ : PR can only be 3 : 8 or 3 : 2
items.reasoning: Let PQ = 3k and QR = 5k. Three points on a line admit three orderings. If Q lies between P and R, then PR = PQ + QR = 8k and PQ : PR = 3 : 8. If P lies between Q and R, then QR = QP + PR, so 5k = 3k + PR, giving PR = 2k and PQ : PR = 3 : 2. If R lies between P and Q, then PQ = PR + RQ, so 3k = PR + 5k and PR = -2k, which is impossible for a length; this case is ruled out because QR is longer than PQ. Two valid configurations give two distinct ratios, so n = 2.

items.value: 6 ways: each of the two main diagonals of 8 squares contains 3 runs of 6 consecutive squares
items.reasoning: A diagonal of L squares contains L - 6 + 1 runs of 6 consecutive squares. Each main diagonal of a chessboard has 8 squares, giving 8 - 6 + 1 = 3 runs, and there are two main diagonals, so 3 x 2 = 6. The reading is pinned down by the options: if every diagonal of the board were allowed, the diagonals of length 6, 7 and 8 in each direction would give (1 + 1) + (2 + 2) + 3 = 9 per direction and 18 in all, which is not offered, so the question means the two main diagonals. The runner-up is D (12), which would win if the paper treats a run and its reverse as two different 'ways', i.e. counts directed paths; the word 'chosen' points to an unordered selection, so 6 is taken.

items.value: ababab; the completed series is the block abbaab repeated three times
items.reasoning: The series has 18 characters with blanks at positions 1, 3, 5, 8, 10 and 15. Filling them with a, b, a, b, a, b in that order gives abbaab abbaab abbaab, a single six-letter block repeated three times, and every one of the twelve letters already printed agrees with it. The other three choices were tested the same way and none produces a repeating block: A gives bbaabb / aabbab / abaaab, B gives bbaaab / abbbab / abaaab, and C gives bbbaab / aabbab / abbaab. Only D yields a specific order, so it is unique.

items.value: 6 such numbers
items.reasoning: The five digits 2, 2, 3, 3, 3 give 5!/(2!3!) = 10 distinct five-digit arrangements. Since the only digits available are 2 and 3, a number exceeds 30000 exactly when its leading digit is 3; a leading 2 gives a number below 30000. Fixing 3 in front leaves 2, 2, 3, 3 to arrange, which can be done in 4!/(2!2!) = 6 ways. The six numbers are 32233, 32323, 32332, 33223, 33232 and 33322.

For statement 1, five consecutive integers starting at n sum to 5n + 10; setting this equal to 100 gives n = 18, and 18 + 19 + 20 + 21 + 22 = 100, so the sum can indeed be 100. For statement 2, n(n+1)(n+2) = 3(n+1) reduces to n(n+2) = 3, i.e. n^2 + 2n - 3 = 0, whose roots are n = 1 and n = -3; the natural-number root n = 1 gives 1 x 2 x 3 = 6 and 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, so the product does equal the sum. Both statements are therefore correct.

items.value: 1000000 millilitres (1 cubic metre = 1000 litres)
items.reasoning: A cube of side 1 m has volume 1 cubic metre. One cubic metre equals 1000 litres, because 1 litre is 1000 cubic centimetres and 1 cubic metre is 1000000 cubic centimetres. Since 1 litre is 1000 millilitres, the vessel holds 1000 x 1000 = 1000000 mL. Equivalently, 1 cubic centimetre is 1 mL and the cube contains 100 x 100 x 100 = 1000000 of them.

items.value: 4 combinations
items.reasoning: Choosing 3 of 6 people in a row with no two adjacent is the standard count C(n - k + 1, k) = C(6 - 3 + 1, 3) = C(4, 3) = 4. Listing them by position confirms it: {1,3,5}, {1,3,6}, {1,4,6} and {2,4,6} are the only selections in which no two chosen positions are next to each other.

items.value: Only statement 1 is correct: p > q + r forces A's share to be the largest, but r < p + q does not force C's share to be the smallest
items.reasoning: Shares are in the ratio p : q : r with all parts positive. If p > q + r, then since r > 0 we get p > q, and since q > 0 we get p > r, so A's share is the largest and statement 1 holds. Statement 2 fails on a simple counterexample: take p : q : r = 1 : 1 : 1.5. Here r = 1.5 is less than p + q = 2, yet C's share is the largest, not the smallest. The condition r < p + q only bounds r against the other two combined, which is far too weak to make r the smallest of the three.

items.value: People open new frontiers chiefly for economic reasons, not out of science or curiosity
items.reasoning: The passage states directly that historically the driver for opening frontiers has always been the search for resources and that science and curiosity are weaker drivers, illustrating this with Silk Road merchants and Portuguese caravels sailing for gold and spices rather than knowledge. Option C is that claim. Option A overreaches to 'any human endeavour', where the passage speaks only of opening frontiers. Option B inverts the argument: the passage says an economic engine will open up space, not that space will govern the economy. Option D also inverts it, making wealth a product of risk-taking when the passage makes the prospect of wealth the reason the risk was taken.

items.value: The first part reports an agreement, held by most people, about telling lies being wrong
items.reasoning: The opening clause is 'most people would agree that telling deliberate lies is wrong'. That is an agreement, and its subject is the telling of lies, which is precisely option A. Options B, C and D all describe a disagreement, and no disagreement is reported anywhere in the first part; the qualifying phrase about special situations where more harm follows from telling the truth is an exception attached to the same shared view, not a dispute about it.

items.value: Even very truthful people habitually mix truth with falsehood in their use of words, the semantic lie
items.reasoning: The passage says that even the most truthful people tell semantic lies and that their use of words contains some measure of falsehood, which is a mixing of the true and the false, so option A fits. Option B, the runner-up, adds 'intentional', and the passage deliberately hedges on that: the falsehood is described as 'more or less deliberate', and the preceding sentence has already separated deliberate lies, which most people agree are wrong, from the semantic lies of truthful people. B would win only if 'more or less deliberate' is read as meaning always deliberate to some degree rather than as a hedge. Option C, falsification of facts, and option D, complete concealment of truth, both go far beyond 'some measure of falsehood' in the use of words.

items.value: p = 30 per cent, so the sector angle is 108 degrees
items.reasoning: The three components must total 100 per cent, so other dry elements account for 100 - 16 - 70 = 14 per cent. Proteins together with the other dry elements therefore give p = 16 + 14 = 30 per cent, which is simply everything that is not water. A sector of a pie diagram takes the same fraction of 360 degrees as its share of the whole, so the central angle is 30/100 x 360 = 108 degrees.

items.value: They meet again after 360 days, which is a Wednesday
items.reasoning: All three are at the club together on days that are common multiples of 5, 24 and 9, so the next such day is the LCM. Factorising, 5 = 5, 24 = 2^3 x 3 and 9 = 3^2, so the LCM is 2^3 x 3^2 x 5 = 360 days. Dividing 360 by 7 leaves a remainder of 3 (since 51 x 7 = 357), so the day is 3 weekdays after Sunday, namely Wednesday.

items.value: Both are correct: the digits differ by 6, and the sum is pinned down once the product is known
items.reasoning: Writing the number as 10a + b, the difference from its reverse is (10a + b) - (10b + a) = 9(a - b) = 54, so a - b = 6 and statement 2 is correct outright. That leaves exactly four possibilities: (6,0), (7,1), (8,2) and (9,3), with sums 6, 8, 10, 12 and products 0, 7, 16, 27. The sums are all different, so the sum is not determined by the given information alone; the products are also all different, so supplying the product identifies the pair and hence the sum. Statement 1 is therefore correct as intended. The runner-up is B (2 only), which would win on a strict reading of 'only if' as an exclusivity claim, since other information such as either digit would also fix the sum; that reading treats statement 1 as overreaching.

items.value: Y is 14 and X is 42; statement 1 fails (34 is not 5 x 6) while statement 2 holds (56 = 2 x 28)
items.reasoning: If Y's present age is y, then X's age when Y was born was 42 - y, and the remark sets that equal to twice Y's present age: 42 - y = 2y, so y = 14. Check: X was 28 at Y's birth, which is twice 14. Statement 1: eight years ago X was 34 and Y was 6, and 5 x 6 = 30, not 34, so it is false. Statement 2: after 14 years X will be 56 and Y will be 28, and 56 = 2 x 28, so it is true. Only statement 2 is correct.

items.value: No net change; the price returns to its original value
items.reasoning: Take the original price as 100. A 20 per cent decrease gives 80. Increasing 80 by 25 per cent adds 20, returning the price to 100. Algebraically the two factors are 0.8 x 1.25 = 1 exactly, because 1.25 is the reciprocal of 0.8, so the net change is 0 per cent. Option D is wrong because percentage changes are multiplicative and need no absolute price to be resolved.

The product must be a repunit, a number written entirely with ones. Testing them in order, 1, 11, 111, 1111 and 11111 leave remainders on division by 7, but 111111 = 7 x 15873 exactly, so 15873 is the smallest such multiplier. Checking the alternatives confirms it: 15713 x 7 = 109991, 15723 x 7 = 110061 and 15783 x 7 = 110481, none of which consists only of ones.

items.value: 15 more days; 5/8 of the original job remains at a rate of 1/24 per day
items.reasoning: Completing 7/8 of the job in 21 days means the whole original job would take 24 days, so his rate is 1/24 of the original job per day. Increasing the quantum of work by 50 per cent makes the total 3/2 of the original job, of which he has already done 7/8, leaving 3/2 - 7/8 = 5/8 to do. At 1/24 per day that takes (5/8) x 24 = 15 days. Note that increasing only the remaining 1/8 by 50 per cent would give 4.5 days, which is not among the options, confirming that the increase applies to the whole job.
